--- title: "Local resolution weighted composite of Martigny" guide-section: "Tutorials" bread-crumbs: false execute: freeze: true --- # Local resolution weighted composite of Martigny This tutorial runs the whole pipeline, from search to composites, for an area around Martigny in the Swiss canton of Valais. The town is surrounded by mountains, whose steep slopes are challenging terrain for SAR. The tutorial compares a composite of the ascending orbits, one of the descending orbits, and one that combines both with local resolution weighting (LRW). ## Find the grid square and its bursts The area lies in one 10 km square of the MGRS grid. The search covers the square whole, as in [From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#find-the-bursts-of-every-square), and keeps the VV bursts of August 2025 that reach it: ::: {#99915ecc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from shapely.geometry import box from s1bursts import ( BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter, RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange, ) fm = FileManager("data/martigny") catalog = BurstCatalog(fm) aoi = box(7.01, 46.09, 7.055, 46.125) window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31") (square,) = MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20) # the area lies in one square print(square.mgrs_code, square.crs) search_area = box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox) found = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV")) bursts = found.intersecting(square) bursts.df.groupby(["pass_direction", "rel_orbit_number"]).agg( acquisitions=("date", lambda dates: dates.dt.date.nunique()), bursts=("burst_id", "size"), sub_swaths=("sub_swath", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.unique()))), satellites=("parent_product_name", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.str[:3].unique()))), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 32TLS40 EPSG:32632 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
acquisitions bursts sub_swaths satellites
pass_direction rel_orbit_number
Ascending 88 5 10 IW2 S1A, S1C
Descending 66 5 10 IW3 S1A, S1C
139 5 15 IW1, IW2 S1A, S1C
``` ::: ::: One ascending and two descending orbits cover the square, each imaged five times in August, with 35 bursts in total. ## Process the bursts The bursts are processed in the UTM zone of the square, at the 20 m pixel size of the composites: ::: {#bab45fe5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure() processor = BurstProcessor(fm) rtc = processor.create_backscatter( bursts, crs=square.crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20), ).raise_on_failure().products ``` ::: ## Compose the square The square is composed twice: once per pass direction with `compose_rtc_by_pass()`, and once across both directions with `compose_rtc_lrw()`, which also writes the quality layers. For an area of several squares, [From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#compose-each-square) loops over them. ::: {#5cc53e71 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm) lrw = weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window) by_pass = weighter.compose_rtc_by_pass(rtc, square, time_range=window) ``` ::: ## Compare the viewing directions Sentinel-1 looks to the right of its track: east on ascending passes, west on descending ones. A slope facing the radar is squeezed into few pixels and seen coarsely. A slope facing away is stretched and seen finely, unless it is so steep that it lies in radar shadow, where that direction has no value. ::: {#99addfe3 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import rasterio from s1bursts.product import Layer def read(composite, layer=Layer.MEASUREMENT): """Read one layer of a composite, with its extent in kilometers for imshow.""" with rasterio.open(fm.get_product_path(composite, layer)) as src: left, bottom, right, top = (v / 1000 for v in src.bounds) return src.read(1).astype("float32"), [left, right, bottom, top] view = (346, 350, 5106, 5110) # easting and northing in km, UTM zone 32N composites = { "Ascending": read(by_pass["Ascending"]), "Descending": read(by_pass["Descending"]), "LRW": read(lrw), } viridis = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy() viridis.set_bad("white") # pixels without a value: radar shadow fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.2), sharey=True, layout="constrained") for ax, (name, (data, extent)) in zip(axes, composites.items()): image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(data), extent=extent, cmap=viridis, vmin=-15, vmax=0) ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:]) axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)") fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Gamma-0 (dB)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Backscatter composites of August 2025 in a 4 by 4 km window west of Martigny: the five ascending acquisitions (left), the ten descending acquisitions (middle), and all fifteen combined with LRW (right). White marks radar shadow, where a composite has no value.](martigny-composite_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=740 height=266} ::: ::: Each pass composite has gaps on the steep slopes facing away from its direction, and smears the slopes facing it into coarse streaks. The LRW composite has a value everywhere, and on each slope it leans toward the direction that sees the slope finely. ## Read the quality layers The LRW composite comes with two quality layers, shown here for the same window: ::: {#49c74d9d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} layers = { "LRW composite (dB)": (Layer.MEASUREMENT, dict(cmap="viridis", vmin=-15, vmax=0)), "Number of observations": (Layer.QA_NUM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=15)), "Composite quality map (dB)": (Layer.QA_CQM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=-8, vmax=8)), } fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.8), sharey=True, layout="constrained") for ax, (title, (layer, style)) in zip(axes, layers.items()): data, extent = read(lrw, layer) if layer != Layer.QA_NUM: data = 10 * np.log10(data) fig.colorbar(ax.imshow(data, extent=extent, **style), ax=ax, orientation="horizontal") ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:]) axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The LRW composite (left), the number of observations (middle), and the composite quality map in decibels (right).](martigny-composite_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=744 height=322} ::: ::: The number of observations (`QA-NUM`) counts the acquisitions that contribute to each pixel: all fifteen almost everywhere, fewer where one direction sees only radar shadow. The composite quality map (`QA-CQM`) rates the combined resolution of each pixel. It is highest on slopes that some orbits see from behind and lowest on the steepest slopes, which every orbit sees squeezed or not at all. A pixel with a low quality describes the ground more coarsely than its 20 m pixel size suggests. [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains both layers. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Run details Run on 02 November 2026 with s1bursts 0.7.1.dev35+g189a2f464.d20261102 and ESA SNAP 13.0.0. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025). :::
